chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Talha ibn Zayd, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

The Polytheists raided the free-pasture land of Medina, so a caller called out in it, 'O evil morning!' So the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) heard it while among the cavalry, so he rode his horse in pursuit of the enemy. The first of his companions to catch up with him was Abu Qatada on his horse. And beneath the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) was a saddle whose two pads were of fine linen, containing neither roughness nor pride.

So he sought the enemy but they did not encounter anyone, and the cavalry followed him in succession. So Abu Qatada said, 'O Messenger of Allah, the enemy has dispersed. If you see fit, let us race.' He said, 'Yes.' So they raced, and the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) came out first among them. Then he turned towards them and said, 'I am the son of the 'Awateek from Quraysh. It is the steed of the ocean,' meaning his horse.
ai.seo_question: What does the Prophet's horse race and his description of his horse reveal about his character and the nature of his mount?
ai.summary: This narration from *Al-Kafi* highlights the Prophet’s (peace be upon him) mastery of horsemanship and his characteristic humility, as he declared himself 'the son of the old mare' to emphasize his horse's lineage rather than his own status. The mention of the simple leather saddle (*sarf*) devoid of pride (*batar*) serves as a practical model for the Shia concept of *zuhd* (asceticism) amidst worldly power. It underscores the virtue of maintaining readiness for battle while cultivating a modest spirit, a key theme in the chapter on merits of cavalry.

en.hubeali:
Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad Bin Yahya, from Talha Bin Zayd, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> having said:

‘The Polytheists raided upon a free-pasture land of Al-Medina, so a caller among it called out, ‘O evil morning’. So Rasool-Allah<sup>saww</sup> heard it among the cavalry, so he<sup>saww</sup> rode out on his<sup>saww</sup> horse in seeking of the enemy, and the first of his<sup>saww</sup> companions to catch up with him<sup>saww</sup> was Abu Qatada upon a horse of his. And there was a saddle of palm leaves beneath him<sup>saww</sup>, not having anything superficial or pride-worthy.

So he<sup>saww</sup> sought the enemy but did not come across any, and the (Muslim) cavalry followed him<sup>saww</sup> up. So Abu Qatada said, ‘O Rasool-Allah<sup>saww</sup>! The enemy has disperse, so I think we should race back’. So he<sup>saww</sup> said: ‘Yes’. So they raced back and Rasool-Allah<sup>saww</sup> came first over them all. Then he<sup>saww</sup> turned towards them, so he<sup>saww</sup> said: ‘I<sup>saww</sup> am a son<sup>saww</sup> of the ‘Awateek’ from Qureysh. It is steed of the ocean’, meaning his<sup>saww</sup> horse’.
en.sarwar: 15. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father from ibn abu ‘ Umayr from Hafs ibn af-Bakhtariy who has said the following: “Abu ‘ Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, would take part in horse racing contests and sharp-shooting.”
